abstract: |
  The One Health approach promotes collaboration across disciplines to enhance the health of humans, animals, plants, and the environment. Recently developed by the Quadripartite organizations, the One Health Joint Plan of Action (2022-2029) supports countries in adopting the One Health approach through six action tracks. The tracks address multiple aspects of biodiversity, containing guiding actions on: One Health capacity-building (track 1), zoonotic diseases (tracks 2 and 3), food and agriculture (track 4), antimicrobial resistance (track 5), and environmental health (track 6). However, there are currently no indicators for monitoring the implementation, state and progress of these tracks. Our research examines the extent to which they could be assessed by the existing monitoring framework of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF) of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). We evaluated (1) the link between each indicator of the KM-GBF monitoring framework and human, animal, plant, and environmental health, respectively, and (2) the usability of these indicators for monitoring the action tracks. We found that 75% of the KM-GBF indicators are associated with either human (56%), animal (53%), plant (51%), or environmental (63%) health, and that 91% of them could potentially be used for monitoring at least one action track. Reusing existing indicators alleviates the costs associated with the development and measurement of new indicators, thus improving the efficiency of monitoring systems. Our work supports the idea that multilateral progress on the monitoring of biodiversity, through its indissociability from all facets of health, provides a way to retrospectively and prospectively measure progress on ambitious One Health actions.

# Introduction

Human health responds to changes in biodiversity in complex and sometimes contradictory ways [@Robinson2024Biodiversity]. On one hand, biodiversity supplies food, shelter, and medicine that are vital to human health [@Diaz2018Assessing]. On the other hand, infectious diseases originating in wildlife are a serious threat to human health, the transmission of pathogens from animals to humans being a major cause of disease outbreaks [@Jones2008Global]. Ecosystem services, such as climate stabilization, air and water filtration, and natural hazards mitigation, support human societies by maintaining safe and adequate environmental conditions [@Jackson2013Linking]. However, animal and plant diseases can hinder ecosystem services, e.g. through food contamination or the reduction in food production [@Al-Sadi2017Impact]. The main threats to biodiversity (biological invasions, climate change, habitat loss, overexploitation, and pollution @Bellard2022Rankinga) all impact human health, notably by driving the emergence of infectious diseases [@Carlson2025Pathogens]. Because biodiversity and human health are highly interconnected, both can be monitored using a similar set of tools [@Poisot2025Biodiversity].

The One Health approach [@PanelOHHLEP2022Onea; @Winkler2025Lancet] recognizes the importance of biodiversity for public health [@Winkler2025Lancet]. It addresses complex public health challenges at the interface between human, animal, plant, and environmental health [@Rabinowitz2013Linksa] by calling for a paradigm shift in governance, finance, capacity-building, and knowledge transfer and production, while promoting collaboration between health professionals, veterinarians, and biologists. The One Health Joint Plan of Action (OH JPA) (2022-2026, recently extended to 2029) is an action-oriented framework aimed at advancing One Health principles by 2029 [@Organization2022One]. Developed by the Quadripartite organizations, which is a strategic partnership between the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), and the World Health Organization (WHO), the OH JPA contains 19 actions that countries can take to improve One Health capacity-building, political commitment, governance structure, funding, and knowledge systems. These actions form six tracks that collectively seek to strengthen health systems (track 1), prevent zoonotic epidemics and pandemics (track 2), control endemic zoonotic, neglected tropical and vector-borne diseases (track 3), improve food safety (track 4), reduce antimicrobial resistance (track 5), and integrate the environment into One Health (track 6). As we enter the last few years of the plan, there is a need to generate clear and objective information regarding the progress made since its adoption in 2022. This evaluation is essential given the non-binding nature of the OH JPA, as it would encourage effective policy development by the States and inform the development of the next version of the plan. However, there are currently no indicators for monitoring the implementation of this plan.

Biodiversity indicators are measures of changes in the state of biodiversity over time that track progress towards specific objectives [@Jones2011Why; @Hebert2025Selectinga]. As such, they are intended to serve several purposes, the main ones being to simplify complex phenomena which are difficult to measure directly, and to improve accountability and effectiveness through prioritization, evaluation and communication of objectives and policies [@Gudmundsson2003Policy; @Nicholson2012Making; @Amuasi2025Future]. A solid example of monitoring framework can be found in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF) [@KMGBF], adopted in 2022 by the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). The KM-GBF aims to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030 through 4 general goals and 23 specific targets, ranging from the restoration of degraded ecosystems to the integration of biodiversity in decision-making. For the first time since the CBD was signed in 1992, the KM-GBF includes a monitoring framework [@Monitoring] made up of 204 indicators that countries can use to monitor these goals and targets. These indicators are classified in four groups: headline (high-level), binary (yes/no questions), component (technical), and complementary (supporting) indicators. Only two of these groups (headline and binary indicators) are mandatory when reporting national progress to the CBD. This reliance on policy evaluation and indicators is in line with a broader trend that some refer to as an "indicator industry" [@Lehtonen2015Chapter], which aims to provide more precise and quantitative assessments of policies. The CBD serves as a good example of how such indicators constitute "soft instruments" capable of incentivizing States to act when the international agreement is not legally binding [@Kirsop-Taylor2022Chapter]. 

More recently, the Parties to the CBD also adopted the Global Action Plan on Biodiversity and Health (GAP-BH), which formally recognizes the links between biodiversity and human health [@Global]. The GAP-BH groups the targets of the KM-GBF into 14 thematic categories, encompassing a variety of topics ranging from "Land and sea use" (category 1) to "Knowledge and engagement of people" (category 14). Each thematic category has its own relevance to human health. For example, the targets that fall under the "Land and sea use" category, which include the "restoration of 30% of all degraded ecosystems" (target 2) and the "conservation of 30% of land, waters and seas" (target 3), contribute to "the continued provision of nature’s contributions to people, which in turn support health and reduce disease emergence and transmission among wildlife, livestock and people" [@Global]. Because of the high relevance of all KM-GBF targets to human health as described in the GAP-BH, we hypothesized that a large proportion of the indicators of these targets would also be relevant to health, and therefore to the retrospective and prospective monitoring of the OH JPA. Given the recent increase in prominence of the One Health approach following its introduction in the Article 5 of the WHO Pandemic Agreement [@Who], it is also crucial to anticipate on the reporting need of a future high-level document for One Health (which could e.g. be adopted at a future Conference of the Parties) and to suggest existing indicators and reporting processes that could support its implementation.

We argue that reusing indicators for both monitoring systems (the KM-GBF and the OH JPA) would improve their efficiency and reduce the workload of countries. During the vote of the KM-GBF monitoring framework, delegates warned that too many indicators could hinder monitoring, especially in less well-resourced nations [@Carroll2024Lessons]. Colinas et al. @Colinas2026Issuesa present best practices in developing indicators for monitoring One Health. They suggest to review existing indicators rather than devoting resources to designing a new standardized and aggregated single index such as the One Health Index [@deMoura2022One] and the Global One Health Index [@Zhang2022Global]. Our work serves as a first step in the framework they propose by quantifying the extent to which the OH JPA is already covered by existing biodiversity indicators in the KM-GBF. Moreover, in the absence of a prior monitoring system, many of the KM-GBF indicators still lack an agreed-upon methodology, both at the national and international levels [@Affinito2025Assessinga]: a further reason why pooling efforts would help improve both this framework and the OH JPA. Despite these difficulties, the indicators of the KM-GBF have ultimately achieved a broad global consensus, and this grants them an important legitimacy as reporting instruments in other context, whenever they are relevant. Therefore, our study aimed to identify the indicators of the KM-GBF that could support the assessment of the OH JPA. First, we assessed the link between each of these indicators and human, animal, plant, and environmental health, respectively. Then, we evaluated the potential usability of the indicators for monitoring the specific action tracks of the OH JPA. Our work highlights the important role of biodiversity monitoring in effective One Health strategies.

# Methods

We qualitatively assessed the relevance of all KM-GBF indicators [@Monitoring] to health. Specifically, we evaluated the degree to which the indicators are linked to each of the four pillars of One Health (i.e., to human, animal, plant, and environmental heath), as well as their potential usability for monitoring the OH JPA. This was done independently by two evaluators for each of the indicators, this process leading to a consensus among the coauthors for all indicators. The first author assessed all 204 indicators, while three other coauthors shared and independently reassessed an equal portion of the indicators based on their area of expertise, providing a brief justification for each indicator. Our assessments were informed by the metadata (rationale, definition, method of computation, data sources, and scale of use) of the indicators provided by the World Conservation Monitoring Centre of the UN Environment Programme [@Indicators], when available, looking for explicit considerations of health. When such metadata was unavailable, assessments were supplemented by expert elicitation. No formal scoring rubric or specific criteria were used to prioritize open-ended, nuanced, and indicator-specific justifications. Our assessments were also guided by the definitions of human, animal, plant, and environmental health provided in Boxes 1 and 2. Small disagreements between the evaluators (assessments in adjacent classes) were resolved by systematically retaining the coauthor's classification. For larger disagreements, the first author reevaluated his original assessments based on the justifications provided by the coauthors. The final classifications were reviewed and approved by all of the coauthors. The spreadsheet containing the assessment results is provided in the Supplementary Materials.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
### Box 1: What are animals, plants, and the environment in One Health?

The definitions of animals, plants, and the environment in One Health are based more on institutional norms than on biological realities. Here, we adhere to the delineation of these groups by mandates of the four organizations that form the Quadripartite. Humans are their own pillar of One Health and the primary focus of the WHO. Animals and plants refer to *domesticated* species only, a distinction we make to align more closely with the mandates of the WOAH (animals) and FAO (plants). Therefore, we include pets, livestock, and edible marine and freshwater species captured from fisheries and aquaculture in the animal health pillar, i.e. species mainly looked after by veterinarians and food inspectors. Even though, biologically speaking, humans and wildlife are also animals, they are not part of the animal health pillar. Similarly, we include all cultivated plants used for food, fuel, and medicine into the plant health pillar. Wildlife and uncultivated plant species, such as wild fish and tree species used in forestry, are part of the environment health pillar, alongside all other species absent from the other three pillars. The environment health pillar also includes whole ecosystems (natural and artificial), which are central to UNEP's mission. These definitions are aligned with the core contributing sciences of the One Health approach, i.e. human medicine, veterinary medicine, agriculture, and ecology [@Gibbs2014Evolution; @Lerner2017Comparison]. While it may be biologically frustrating to work within this framework, we emphasize that assigning groups of organisms to specific organizations has the direct benefit of inscribing our work within established systems of governance and reporting.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
### Box 2: What is health?

Throughout this manuscript, we use the overarching term "health" when referring to the health of different species and the environment, and refer to human, animal, plant, and environmental health when wanting to differentiate. Health emerges differently depending on the level of biological organization [@Lerner2015Concept]. At the individual level, we use the WHO definition of health that considers the overall well-being of individuals and their capacity to function normally, which includes the absence of diseases [@Preamble]. In humans and domestic and wildlife animals, well-being is the ability for an individual to satisfy its physical, mental, and behavioral needs [@Webb2019What], whereas diseases are undesirable conditions often leading to pain, suffering, or death. This is addressed, in the spirit of One Health, holistically at the individual, populational, and global scale, and therefore accounts for _e.g._ health system preparedness. In plants, which are not conscious organisms [@Mallatt2021Debunking], health is the extent to which they are able to function physiologically, and diseases are impediments to their normal physiological functioning often leading to death [@Doring2012Concepts]. Recent developments in One Health supplement the WHO definition by highlighting the dynamic nature of health from a socioecological perspective, particularly the capacity of an individual to adapt, recover, and maintain biological functioning under changing environmental conditions [@PanelOHHLEP2022Onea; @Winkler2025Lancet]. At the ecosystem level, consisting of many species and their interactions, health is ill-defined [@Schaeffer1988Ecosystem]. The idea of ecosystem health, although ancient in Indigenous and non-Western cosmological perspectives [@Hierro2005Land; @Descola2013Nature], has often been promoted as metaphorical [@Rapport1989What; @Costanza1999What]. We consider environmental health as the extent to which an ecosystem can maintain its biological and chemical processes, adapt to changes, and sustain the conditions underpinning human, animal, and plant health [@Jakobsson2012Sustainable]. Healthy ecosystems are often characterized by high levels of ecological integrity and biodiversity [@Ostfeld2017Biodiversity]. Disturbances, such as extreme weather events or resource exploitation, are the ecosystem analogue of diseases, and represent degradations that usually lead to a decline in ecosystem functioning. Environmental health also includes the health of species that are part of the environment pillar of One Health, e.g. wildlife and uncultivated plant species.
:::


## Assessing the link between KM-GBF indicators and health

We classified the degree to which the KM-GBF indicators are linked to each of the four pillars of One Health into four categories: direct connection, indirect connection, potential connection, and no connection. An indicator was classified as directly connected to health when there is a direct causal relationship between the indicator and health. This is the case, for instance, when the indicator is a direct measure of health, a determinant of health (e.g., an ecological, social, political, cultural, or economic determinant of health), or a management intervention that directly impacts health. Considering these cases together is consistent with the approach adopted by the KM-GBF monitoring framework, which does not explicitly distinguish between indicators measuring the state of biodiversity, the environmental and anthropogenic pressures on biodiversity, our responses to biodiversity loss, and the benefits people receive from nature [@ExpertInput2022]. In contrast, an indicator was classified as indirectly connected to health when there is an intermediary factor between the indicator and the measure or determinant of health, and as potentially connected when there are multiple intermediary factors or when its connection to health is likely but difficult to certify. Finally, an indicator was classified as not connected to health when the connection is unlikely, unsupported by current scientific evidence, or absent. For each of the four pillars of One Health, we counted the number of indicators assigned to each category.

For example, headline indicator 7.2 "Pesticide environment concentration and/or aggregated total applied toxicity" was considered directly connected to human health because it directly measures an environmental determinant of health, many pesticides being toxic to humans under high level of exposure [@Kim2017Exposure]. It was also considered directly connected to animal, plant, and environmental health because its use can directly impact the health of many species in an ecosystem. The use of pesticides can benefit the growth of cultivated plants through the reduction of herbivory and competition, while simultaneously harming plant health through their phytotoxicity. Pesticides may also be harmful to some animal populations and the broader agroecosystem by disrupting vital biological and ecological functions [@Mahmood2016Effects]. In contrast, component indicator 4.CT.1 "Number of plant and animal genetic resources for food and agriculture secured in either medium- or long-term conservation facilities" was considered indirectly connected to human health because the potential health impact of this intervention occurs through an intermediary factor. Conserving genetic resources increases the resilience of food systems to global disasters [@Esquinas-Alcazar2005Protecting], which in turn protects human health. However, we did not find any evidence of a link between this indicator and animal, plant, or environmental health.


## Assessing the usability of KM-GBF indicators for monitoring the OH JPA action tracks

For each action track of the OH JPA, we classified the KM-GBF indicators into three categories: directly usable, usable after adaptation, and not usable. Directly usable indicators have the potential to be used in their current form to monitor the implementation of at least one action in an action track. They can detect trends relevant to the actions of the track and do not require adaptations. For example, we qualified headline indicator 7.2 "Pesticide environment concentration and/or aggregated total applied toxicity" as being directly usable for monitoring the sixth action track because it is a direct measure of environmental degradation and contamination. In contrast, indicators usable after adaptation need to be slightly modified before being used to monitor actions in an action track. These adaptations should be small changes in the scale of measurement, the data resolution, the methodology or the taxa monitored by the indicator. For instance, headline indicator 7.2 was qualified as being usable after adaptation for monitoring the fourth action track on food safety risks. To be more relevant for this action track, this indicator could be restricted to the use of pesticides in agricultural areas rather than the whole environment. Finally, not usable indicators are outside the scope of an action track or need to be greatly modified before being used to monitor the implementation of an action track. Headline indicator 7.2, for example, was classified as being not usable for the third action track on endemic zoonotic, neglected tropical, and vector-borne diseases. Adapting this indicator to the third action track would require substantial changes to its data collection and methodology. Specifically, it would need to focus on the public health use of pesticides in treated areas and assess the risks on selected vector groups. To determine whether the required adaptations were minor or major, we assessed whether adapting the existing indicator to the action track would require more efforts and resources than creating and monitoring an entirely new indicator. These three categories (directly usable, usable after adaptation, and not usable) represent the conceptual relevance and potential usability of indicators, not their demonstrated capacity to monitor actions. Metrics of indicator quality such as validity, reliability, sensitivity, specificity, feasibility, data completeness, and outcome attribution, which should be evaluated before using existing indicators for a new purpose, are not considered in the current study.

We assessed potential usability for each action track independently, i.e. an indicator could potentially be useful for monitoring multiple action tracks. For each action track, we counted the total number of indicators in each category. We also counted the number of potentially usable indicators for the whole plan regardless of the action tracks. Then, we partitioned these numbers based on the group of indicators in the KM-GBF monitoring framework (i.e. headline, binary, component, and complementary indicators) and the thematic categories of the GAP-BH. Finally, for each action track where an indicator was considered potentially usable (either directly or after adaptation), we identified the most relevant action that could be monitored by the indicator, and counted the number of indicators associated with each action.

# Results and discussion

## Link between KM-GBF indicators and health

We found that 75% of KM-GBF indicators are either directly or indirectly connected to either human, animal, plant, or environmental health, with approximately 55% of indicators being directly connected to health. This signifies that monitoring the state, benefits, and pressure on biodiversity and our responses to biodiversity loss provides extensive health information. In @fig-link, we show the number of indicators that are directly, indirectly, potentially, and not connected to each of the four pillars of One Health. The number of directly connected indicators is, as expected, slightly higher for environmental health (41% of indicators) compared to human (27%), animal (26%), and plant (28%) health, mostly because the environment contains most of biodiversity. However, this difference is less pronounced after adding indirectly connected indicators (63% for environmental health compared to 56%, 53%, and 51% respectively for human, animal, and plant health), highlighting the multiple pathways through which biodiversity and health are connected.

![**Number of indicators of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework linked with human, animal, plant, and environmental health.** Each indicator was classified as being either directly connected (blue), indirectly connected (green), potentially connected (orange), or not connected (red) to each of the four pillars of One Health.](figures/link_health.png){#fig-link}

The fact that most KM-GBF indicators are connected to health is not surprising. The GAP-BH recognizes the relevance to health of all 23 targets of the KM-GBF, and because the indicators measure the progress made towards these targets, they also measure the progress made towards a healthier planet. However, we did not expect that comparable numbers of indicators would be linked to the four pillars of One Health, indicating that similar amount of information can be reused, either directly or indirectly, to monitor human, animal, plant, and environmental health. This suggests that the core components of One Health can all be informed by biodiversity monitoring.

## Usability of KM-GBF indicators for monitoring the OH JPA action tracks

The vast majority of KM-GBF indicators (91%) have the potential to be used either directly or after adaptation to monitor the OH JPA action tracks, and around 74% of indicators could potentially be used directly. This suggests that existing KM-GBF indicators may provide a substantial starting point for monitoring many aspects of the OH JPA, although their suitability for evaluating implementation and outcomes would require further validation. However, we show in @fig-use-all that the potential usability of the indicators greatly differs depending on the action track. The proportion of potentially usable indicators varies from 20% for the fifth action track on antimicrobial resistance (4% of potentially directly usable indicators) to 79% for the sixth action track on the integration of the environment into One Health (62% of potentially directly usable indicators). The high proportion of potentially usable indicators for the sixth action track is not surprising given that the KM-GBF is a multilateral environmental agreement that aims to protect species and restore ecosystems. The low proportion of indicators that can potentially monitor actions in the fifth action track could be due to the characteristics of these actions, which are more focused on collaboration, capacity-building and awareness-raising than the decrease and prevention of antimicrobial resistance through biodiversity. Similarly, the actions in the third action track on endemic zoonotic, neglected tropical, and vector-borne diseases, which could potentially be monitored by only 33% of the indicators, are more centered on capacity-building and less on the drivers and inhibitors of infectious diseases, especially in comparison to the actions of the second action track on zoonotic epidemics and pandemics. These differences suggest that, although the KM-GBF monitoring framework could greatly reduce the need to develop, gain expertise in, and monitor new indicators for the OH JPA, additional work is still needed to equally cover all aspects of the plan.

![**Number of indicators of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework that could potentially be used to monitor at least one action in each of the action tracks of the One Health Joint Plan of Action.** The opaque bars represent potentially directly usable indicators, whereas the transparent bars represent those potentially usable after adaptation. The proportion of potentially usable indicators (either directly or after adaptation) for each action track is indicated. The bottom bar and proportion designate the indicators that can potentially monitor at least one action in the whole plan.](figures/usability_all.png){#fig-use-all}

The number of indicators associated with each action in the OH JPA is presented in @tbl-letters. There are high discrepancies in the potential usability of indicators between actions. The total number of potentially usable indicators (either directly or after adaptation) varies from 1 (action 5.3: Strengthen global AMR governance structures) to 108 (action 6.1: Protect, restore, and prevent the degradation of ecosystems and the wider environment). Within a single action track, the biggest differences are found in the sixth action track, where only 12 indicators were associated to action 6.4 whereas 108 indicators were associated to action 6.1 This result shows that the KM-GBF monitoring framework can provide substantial information for some of the actions, but it also further highlights the need to identify or develop new indicators for specific actions of the plan, even within the action tracks that could potentially be monitored by numerous indicators, such as action track 6.

: **Number of indicators of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework that could potentially be used directly and after adaptation to monitor each of the actions of the One Health Joint Plan of Action.** The total number of potentially usable indicators for each action track is indicated in the highlighted blue lines. A specific indicator could be used to monitor multiple action tracks, but only the most relevant action in each action track was identified for each indicator. {#tbl-letters}

Most KM-GBF indicators could potentially be used to monitor the OH JPA action tracks, in each of the groups of indicators in the KM-GBF monitoring framework (@fig-use-cat). We evaluated that 100% of headline indicators (27/27), 93% of binary indicators (14/15), 94% of component indicators (49/52), and 87% of complementary indicators (96/110) could potentially be used, either directly or after adaptation, to monitor at least one action track. Headline and binary indicators are the only two mandatory groups of indicators, i.e. that Parties need to include in their national biodiversity reports. The high proportion of relevant headline and binary indicators is encouraging, because it indicates that the information most likely to figure in national reports could potentially be reusable for evaluating the implementation of the OH JPA. On the other hand, the high reusability of component and complementary indicators, which are currently optional, should be seen as an additional incentive to measure them.

![**Proportion of indicators of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework that could potentially be used to monitor at least one action in each of the action tracks of the One Health Joint Plan of Action, partitioned by the different groups of indicators.** The number of indicators in each group is indicated in parentheses. The opaque bars represent potentially directly usable indicators, whereas the transparent bars represent those potentially usable after adaptation. The gray bars designate the indicators that could potentially monitor at least one action in the whole plan.](figures/usability_categories.png){#fig-use-cat}

For each thematic category of the GAP-BH, at least 89% of indicators could potentially be used, either directly or after adaptation, for monitoring at least one action track, except in the "Knowledge and engagement of people" category, where only 52% of the indicators could potentially be used (@fig-use-GAP). This suggests that every sector of the KM-GBF monitoring framework, from "Nature's contribution to people" to "Species management", could be relevant to the OH JPA, even though there are wide variations in the action track most relevant for each category. For instance, the three indicators under "Urban areas" could only be used after adaptation to monitor the action tracks, apart from tracks 1 and 6, yet they do not capture actions related to antimicrobial resistance (track 5). @fig-use-GAP also shows that all indicators that could potentially directly monitor the fifth action track on antimicrobial resistance are in the "Access and benefit-sharing" and "Biosafety and biotechnology" categories, further emphasizing the importance of collaboration, capacity-building and awareness-raising set forth in this action track.

![**Proportion of indicators of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework that could potentially be used to monitor at least one action in each of the action tracks of the One Health Joint Plan of Action, partitioned by the different thematic categories of the Global Action Plan on Biodiversity and Health.** The number of indicators in each thematic category is indicated in parentheses. The thematic category of an indicator was assigned based on the thematic category of its target. Indicators that monitor goals A, B, C, and D of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework are not assigned to any thematic category. The opaque bars represent potentially directly usable indicators, whereas the transparent bars represent those potentially usable after adaptation. The gray bars designate the indicators that could potentially monitor at least one action in the whole plan.](figures/usability_GAP.png){#fig-use-GAP}

These findings reveal substantial conceptual overlap between the KM-GBF indicators and the OH JPA action tracks. However, these indicators alone cannot capture the full scope of the OH JPA action tracks. The KM-GBF monitoring framework collects information regarding biodiversity, environmental pressures, conservation responses, and nature's contributions to people. In comparison, many OH JPA action tracks focus on governance, capacity-building, financing, policy development, and collaboration across disciplines, sectors, and countries. Therefore, while the KM-GBF indicators provide valuable information on the ecological dimensions of the action tracks, they provide fewer information on their governance and institutional dimensions, as shown by the limited coverage of the third and fifth action tracks. Nevertheless, the KM-GBF indicators could support One Health policy-making by improving our understanding of the interlinkages between biodiversity and health, i.e. they should be used as a diagnostic tool rather than a management tool tailored to the specific actions of the OH JPA [@Hillebrand2025Operationala]. Incorporating biodiversity monitoring into a One Health monitoring programme represents one of several steps towards better accounting for external forces that influence health system performance and policy making, alongside established social, political, cultural, and economic determinants of health.

# Conclusion

This study suggests that a large number of KM-GBF indicators could potentially be used, either directly or after adaptation, to monitor the implementation of the OH JPA action tracks. Instead of developing and measuring new indicators, which can be resource-intensive, these indicators could provide valuable ecological information, provided their quality and suitability for monitoring the OH JPA action tracks are carefully assessed. However, practical challenges regarding the data collection and methodological development of the KM-GBF indicators remain. Many indicators are still under development, lack a clear standardized methodology, are not adequately monitored, or have limited baseline data. We argue that reusing indicators could increase the efficiency of both monitoring systems: the environmental sector could meaningfully contribute to One Health efforts by sharing their data, tools, and expertise, whereas the use of KM-GBF indicators by One Health agencies could provide further incentives to fill gaps in biodiversity data and methodological development. Moreover, as Parties to the CBD submit their National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAPs) with the monitored indicators [@Mechanisms], large amounts of new data will become available for the retrospsective and prospective assessment of the progress made on the ambitious One Health actions. 

Our evaluation of the reusability of KM-GBF indicators for monitoring the OH JPA represents an initial step towards monitoring One Health actions more broadly. Although globally relevant, the OH JPA may not fully reflect local priorities and implementation pathways. The relevance of KM-GBF indicators to other One Health frameworks, such as national One Health strategies and action plans, remains to be assessed. As outlined in our approach, conducting this evaluation could ultimately reduce the workload of countries by making indicators serve more than one purpose, thereby avoiding duplication of work. Additional effort is also needed to identify or develop new indicators to monitor the OH JPA action tracks where few KM-GBF indicators were found to be potentially usable. These gaps could be filled by finding existing indicators in other multilateral environmental agreements, such as the global indicator framework of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Putting in the work to develop comprehensive monitoring frameworks for the OH JPA and other One Health frameworks will be an essential step to ensure they are effectively put into action and meet their goals.
